title: Streamline Flow in Fluids
short_intro: Streamline flow (or laminar flow) is a regime of fluid motion in which each particle of the fluid follows a smooth path, called a streamline, such that the paths of different particles never cross each other. At any given point in the fluid, the velocity vector of the fluid particles remains constant with time in both magnitude and direction.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of streamline, laminar vs turbulent flow, equation of continuity (A1v1 = A2v2), Bernoulli's theorem and its direct applications like Venturi meter and Torricelli's law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Euler's equation of motion for inviscid fluids, derivation of Bernoulli's equation from work-energy theorem, velocity potential and stream function for two-dimensional irrotational flow, vorticity.

prerequisites: Equation of continuity and conservation of mass
Concept of pressure, density, and viscosity in fluids

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Characteristics of Streamlines
bullets: A streamline is an imaginary curve drawn in a fluid flow such that the tangent at any point on the curve gives the direction of the velocity vector of the fluid particle at that point.
Two streamlines can never intersect, because if they did, the fluid particle at the point of intersection would have two different velocity vectors simultaneously, which is physically impossible.
In a steady flow, streamlines coincide with the actual path (trajectory) of individual fluid particles.

concept_notes.heading: Equation of Continuity
bullets: Based on the law of conservation of mass for an incompressible fluid flowing through a tube of varying cross-section.
The product of the cross-sectional area (A) and the fluid velocity (v) remains constant along any streamline: Av = constant.
Physical interpretation: Where the pipe is narrower, the fluid speed is greater; where the pipe is wider, the fluid speed is smaller.

concept_notes.heading: Bernoulli's Theorem
bullets: Derived from the work-energy theorem applied to a non-viscous, incompressible, and streamline fluid flow.
States that the sum of pressure energy per unit volume, kinetic energy per unit volume, and potential energy per unit volume remains constant along a streamline.

concept_notes.heading: Conditions for Streamline Flow
bullets: The flow velocity at any fixed point must not change with time (steady flow condition).
The Reynolds number (R<sub>e</sub>) must remain well below the critical value for the given geometry (typically R<sub>e</sub> < 2000 in pipes).
Fluid viscosity and internal friction must not cause turbulent eddies under the operating flow speed.

derivations.title: Equation of Continuity Derivation
derivations.conditions: Incompressible fluid, steady flow through a rigid pipe of varying cross-section
steps: Consider a section of a pipe with cross-sectional areas A<sub>1</sub> and A<sub>2</sub> at two points 1 and 2.
Let the fluid enter point 1 with speed v<sub>1</sub> and density ρ, and leave point 2 with speed v<sub>2</sub> and density ρ.
Mass entering in time interval dt is dm<sub>1</sub> = ρ A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> dt.
Mass leaving in time interval dt is dm<sub>2</sub> = ρ A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub> dt.
By conservation of mass for an incompressible fluid (ρ<sub>1</sub> = ρ<sub>2</sub> = ρ), dm<sub>1</sub> = dm<sub>2</sub>.

derivations.title: Bernoulli's Equation Derivation
derivations.conditions: Streamline, steady, irrotational flow of an ideal (inviscid and incompressible) fluid
steps: Consider a fluid element moving from a lower cross-section to a higher cross-section under pressure forces and gravity.
Work done by the pressure forces per unit volume during displacement is W<sub>pressure</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> - P<sub>2</sub>.
Work done by gravity against the weight of the fluid element per unit volume is W<sub>gravity</sub> = ρ g h<sub>1</sub> - ρ g h<sub>2</sub>.
By work-energy theorem, total net work done per unit volume equals the change in kinetic energy per unit volume: (&frac{1}{2}ρ v<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> - &frac{1}{2}ρ v<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>).
Rearranging terms by grouping parameters of state 1 on one side and state 2 on the other yields the constant sum.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity Profile in Laminar vs Turbulent Flow
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic velocity profile across the diameter of a pipe for laminar flow, contrasted with a flattened (blunt) profile for turbulent flow.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: In streamline flow, maximum velocity occurs at the center of the pipe and zero velocity occurs at the walls due to no-slip condition.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT/PGT to identify parabolic distribution with maximum velocity at axis.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Venturi Tube Pressure Head Variation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A horizontal pipe constriction connected with vertical manometric tubes showing liquid column heights dropping at the throat.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At the narrower throat, velocity is higher, causing static pressure to drop according to Bernoulli's principle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and theoretical questions regarding pressure difference and manometer height differences.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Reynolds Dye Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic of a glass tank with a central filament of colored dye injected into flowing water.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At low velocities, the dye filament remains a straight, distinct line (streamline flow). Above critical velocity, the filament breaks up into eddies (turbulent flow).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions concerning the criterion for transition from streamline to turbulent flow.

solved_numericals.question: Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose internal diameter changes from 4 cm at point A to 2 cm at point B. If the speed of water at point A is 2 m/s, find the speed of water at point B.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: D<sub>1</sub> = 4 cm, D<sub>2</sub> = 2 cm, v<sub>1</sub> = 2 m/s.
Apply the equation of continuity: A<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub>.
Since area is proportional to the square of diameter: (D<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>)v<sub>1</sub> = (D<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>)v<sub>2</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: A horizontal venturi meter with a throat-to-main-area ratio of 1:2 is used to measure the flow rate of water (ρ = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>). If the manometer fluid indicates a pressure difference of 24 kPa between the main section and the throat, calculate the volume flow rate Q.
solution_steps: Let main area be A<sub>1</sub> and throat area be A<sub>2</sub>. Given A<sub>2</sub>/A<sub>1</sub> = 1/2, so A<sub>1</sub> = 2A<sub>2</sub>.
Use Venturi meter velocity formula for v<sub>1</sub>: v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> √[ 2ΔP / (ρ(A<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> - A_2<sup>2</sup>)) ].

Substitute A<sub>1</sub> = 2A<sub>2</sub>: v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> √[ 2ΔP / (ρ(4A<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> - A<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>)) ] = A<sub>2</sub> √[ 2ΔP / (3ρA<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>) ] = √[ 2ΔP / (3ρ) ].

Volume flow rate Q = A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub>. Alternatively, compute using Q = A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> A<sub>1</sub> √[...] / A<sub>2</sub>. Let us find v<sub>2</sub> from continuity: A<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub> => 2A<sub>2</sub>(4) = A<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub> => v<sub>2</sub> = 8 m/s. Thus Q = A<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> × 8. (Assuming unit area or expressing symbolically if area not given; let's assume A<sub>2</sub> = 0.01 m<sup>2</sup> for numerical completion: Q = 0.01 × 8 = 0.08 m<sup>3</sup>/s).

solved_numericals.question: A small orifice is punched at a depth of 2.0 m below the free surface of water in a large tank. Calculate the velocity of efflux of water from the orifice. (Take g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
solution_steps: Identify depth h = 2.0 m and g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

assumptions_and_limitations: The fluid is assumed to be ideal: non-viscous (zero internal friction) and incompressible (constant density).
The flow must be steady, meaning fluid properties at any point do not vary with time.
Real fluids possess viscosity; hence Bernoulli's equation and streamline relations hold strictly only as approximations away from boundary walls where viscous shear stresses are negligible.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Streamlines represent the physical walls or boundaries of a pipe.
common_misconceptions.correct: Streamlines are purely mathematical curves drawn tangent to velocity vectors inside the fluid body.
common_misconceptions.why: Streamlines exist throughout the fluid continuum, not just at solid boundaries.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Higher fluid velocity implies higher static pressure according to Bernoulli's theorem.
common_misconceptions.correct: Higher fluid velocity corresponds to lower static pressure along a streamline.
common_misconceptions.why: Since kinetic energy per unit volume increases with velocity, static pressure must drop to keep the total sum constant.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Streamlines can intersect if the fluid flow accelerates sharply.
common_misconceptions.correct: Streamlines can never intersect under any steady flow condition.
common_misconceptions.why: Intersection would imply two distinct velocity vectors at a single spatial point for a single fluid particle.

quick_revision: In streamline flow, velocity at any point is constant over time and streamlines never cross.
Equation of Continuity: A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2
Bernoulli's Theorem: P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}
